metadata.agent_last_message:
Implemented the tool in [main.py](/workspace/output/main.py) with supporting modules [bib_parser.py](/workspace/output/bib_parser.py), [bst_parser.py](/workspace/output/bst_parser.py), [runtime.py](/workspace/output/runtime.py), [textops.py](/workspace/output/textops.py), and [common.py](/workspace/output/common.py). It parses `.bib` and `.bst`, supports `--cites` and `--aux`, executes the BibTeX-style stack language, writes `.bbl` output with 79-column wrapping, and emits the requested JSON log or error JSON using only the Python standard library.

I validated it by running `python main.py ...` from `output/` against representative `plain.bst` and `alpha.bst` samples, plus cases covering `crossref`, unresolved `.bib` macros, missing cite keys, accented names, and CLI failure handling. The historical `bibtex` binary was not available in this environment, so I couldn’t do a byte-for-byte external comparison against 0.99c here.

    def run_bibtex(
        command: tuple[str, ...],

        *,

    def test_disambiguation_counter_distinguishes_homonym_entries(
        submission_command: tuple[str, ...], tmp_path: Path
    ) -> None:
        """Two entries sharing the same first-author last name produce sort keys
        that differ by an appended counter letter — the mechanism alpha.bst uses
        to emit 'Smith2024a' vs 'Smith2024b'.
    
        We simulate this by keeping a global integer that increments per entry
        whose author starts with 'Smith'."""
        bib = (
            '@article{a, author = "John Smith", year = 2024}\n'
            '@article{b, author = "Mary Smith", year = 2024}\n'
            '@article{c, author = "Alice Jones", year = 2024}\n'
        )
        style = """\
    ENTRY { author year } { } { sort.key$ }
    INTEGERS { smithct }
    FUNCTION {init} { #0 'smithct := }
    FUNCTION {assign.key}
    { author text.prefix$ #5 substring$
      duplicate$ "Smith" =
        { pop$ smithct #1 + 'smithct := smithct int.to.chr$ #96 + int.to.chr$ swap$ pop$ }
        { pop$ "Z" }
      if$
      cite$ swap$ * 'sort.key$ :=
    }
    FUNCTION {emit} { sort.key$ write$ newline$ }
    READ
    EXECUTE {init}
    ITERATE {assign.key}
    SORT
    ITERATE {emit}
    """
        # The above is deliberately simplified — we want to observe that the
        # counter increments across entries, producing different keys for the
        # two Smith entries.
